title: A Bi-heuristic Initialized NSGA-II Algorithm for Multi-skilled Human-Robot Collaborative Disassembly Line Balancing Considering Robot Technology Tiers and Operator Experience Levels
abstract: The rapid expansion of electric vehicles and renewable energy storage systems has made the efficient recovery of end-of-life batteries a critical global challenge. To support a sustainable circular economy, optimizing human-robot collaborative (HRC) disassembly lines is essential for maximizing resource recovery while controlling operational costs. However, the disassembly line balancing problem (DLBP) is inherently NP-hard, making the optimal assignment of tasks and resources an intractable computational task. In modern hybrid manufacturing environments, integrating multi-skilled (MS) resources with varying robot technology tiers (RTT) and operator experience levels (OEL) is vital, as these factors directly dictate execution speed, flexibility, and total costs. This study proposes a novel bi-objective mixed-integer linear programming model for the MS-HRCDLBP to simultaneously minimize cycle time and total disassembly cost. To solve this problem, the augmented epsilon-constraint (AUGMECON2) algorithm is used to validate the quality of solutions of smaller instances, while a customized hybrid non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (HNSGA-II) with a bi-heuristic initialization strategy is developed for large-scale instances. The proposed approach is validated using an industrial case study on EV battery disassembly, along with adapted benchmark datasets comprising up to 89 tasks. The computational results demonstrate that HNSGA-II effectively overcomes the computational limitations of the exact solver, successfully identifying high-quality Pareto-optimal trade-offs and providing decision-makers with diverse and cost-effective resource allocation strategies.

title: Accelerating Lagrangian Relaxation via Dual-Guided Genetic Search for UAV Trajectory and Camera Orientation Optimization
abstract: This paper addresses unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) path optimization with integrated viewpoint selection and camera orientation planning. The proposed framework captures the intricate interdependencies among these decisions and optimizes them simultaneously for the first time, balancing surface coverage quality and flight energy consumption. To tackle this large-scale combinatorial problem, a Lagrangian relaxation approach decomposes the model into an orienteering subproblem and a coverage subproblem. A Genetic Algorithm (GA) with a dual-guided mutation operator efficiently solves the orienteering subproblem. Theoretical analysis and empirical validation are provided. Experimental results demonstrate that the dual-guided genetic search reduces runtime by 51.3% and improves the weighted objective by 9.3% over a standard genetic algorithm. Moreover, it matches or improves upon an exact mixed-integer linear programming solver while cutting runtime by over 90% on small instances and by 50–70% on larger ones.

title: HCPS: Heuristic Candidate-Space Policy Search for Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling
abstract: Many real-world combinatorial optimization tasks are constrained constructive processes with expensive per-step fitness evaluation. Population-based methods often suffer from high evaluation cost, while single-solution methods may lack exploration. We propose Heuristic Candidate-space Policy Search (HCPS), a hybrid framework that combines heuristic candidate-space shaping with policy-based sequential selection. At each decision step, HCPS applies feasibility-aware Top-K pruning to compress the primitive action space and then uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to optimize long-horizon utility on the reduced candidate set. We provide complexity analysis showing that Top-K pruning can substantially reduce computation while keeping quality loss limited when high-value actions are retained with high probability. Experiments on agile Earth observation satellite scheduling as a representative testbed demonstrate a strong quality–time trade-off and support the framework’s generalizability.

title: Linear Ordering Problem: Time for a Change
abstract: The Linear Ordering Problem (LOP) is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem with important applications in areas such as economics, social choice, and machine learning. Its most prominent use is the triangulation of economic input-output tables, which helps identify critical industries in an economy. Most existing algorithms have been evaluated on benchmarks derived from outdated macroeconomic data, which no longer reflect the structure of contemporary economies. Furthermore, LOP instances often exhibit many distinct global optima that can differ substantially from one another, creating challenges for applications that rely on a single solution. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel benchmark suite derived from up-to-date real-world economic data and an algorithmic scheme that leverages state-of-the-art LOP metaheuristics to generate diverse sets of high-quality solutions, together with metrics for assessing both quality and diversity. Experiments were conducted to report results on the proposed benchmark suite under both the traditional single-solution setting and the newly introduced multi-solution scenario.

title: On the Generalization Bounds of Symbolic Regression with Genetic Programming
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) with genetic programming (GP) aims to discover interpretable mathematical expressions directly from data. Despite its strong empirical success, the theoretical understanding of why GP-based SR generalizes beyond the training data remains limited. In this work, we provide a learning-theoretic analysis of SR models represented as expression trees. We derive a generalization bound for GP-style SR under constraints on tree size, depth, and learnable constants. Our result decomposes the generalization gap into two interpretable components: a structure-selection term, reflecting the combinatorial complexity of choosing an expression-tree structure, and a constant-fitting term, capturing the complexity of optimizing numerical constants within a fixed structure. This decomposition provides a theoretical perspective on several widely used practices in GP, including parsimony pressure, depth limits, numerically stable operators, and interval arithmetic. In particular, our analysis shows how structural restrictions reduce hypothesis-class growth while stability mechanisms control the sensitivity of predictions to parameter perturbations. By linking these practical design choices to explicit complexity terms in the generalization bound, our work offers a principled explanation for commonly observed empirical behaviors in GP-based SR and contributes towards a more rigorous understanding of its generalization properties.

title: Benchmarking Zero-Shot LLM-Generated Parent Selection in Genetic Programming for Symbolic Regression
abstract: Parent selection significantly affects exploration, exploitation, and complexity control in genetic programming (GP) for symbolic regression. It is unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can synthesize effective operators in a zero-shot setting without iterative meta-evolution. Here, zero-shot means that the model receives only the task description, with no reference operators or iterative feedback. In this work, we benchmark zero-shot synthesis of parent-selection operators across eight LLMs within a standard GP framework for symbolic regression. Each model receives the same natural-language prompt to generate a parent-selection operator, which is then evaluated in a standard GP framework with only the parent-selection operator replaced, while all other components and the evolutionary-search budget are held constant. For each LLM, ten independent zero-shot operators are evaluated on twelve OpenML regression benchmarks and compared against automatic lexicase and tournament selection baselines. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro stand out for consistently strong performance on both training and held-out test \(R^2\). The strongest operator in our benchmark—a Kimi K2.5 zero-shot synthesis—surpasses the automatic lexicase and tournament baselines in search effectiveness. These results suggest that zero-shot LLM synthesis is a viable approach to generating competitive GP selection operators. Analysis shows that many generated operators use semantics to guide selection, suggesting that LLMs can produce non-trivial search heuristics from the task description alone. We also examine the relationship between public LLM leaderboard rankings and GP performance. Widely used benchmarks, such as Humanity’s Last Exam and SWE-bench Verified, strongly correlate with training \(R^2\), while their relationship to held-out test \(R^2\) is weaker and less clear.

title: BERT Mutation for Genetic Algorithms: A Deep Transformer Operator
abstract: Traditional genetic algorithm mutation strategies typically apply stochastic gene modifications without considering broader genomic context or learning from historical evolutionary data. To address this, we introduce BERT Mutation for Genetic Algorithms (GAs), a novel, domain-independent contextual mutation operator that adapts the Transformer architecture to fixed-length genetic representations. While deep learning-based operators have shown success in Genetic Programming, extending them to GAs is challenged by “semantic opacity”—the lack of explicit structural definitions in linear integer or binary vectors. To overcome this, we propose a novel data augmentation strategy that generates pseudo-training examples derived from the population’s elite. This strategy enriches the training signal by constructing augmented trajectories toward high-fitness solutions, stabilizing the reinforcement learning process. We evaluate the operator across four diverse domains: Frozen Lake, Artificial Ant, Graph Coloring, and Unweighted Set Cover.Our results demonstrate that BERT Mutation consistently outperforms traditional stochastic operators (One-Point, Uniform, and Zigzag) and an adaptive operator (AOS) in both convergence speed and final solution quality. Notably, BERT Mutation achieves superior average fitness in approximately half the wall-clock time and fewer than half the generations required by competing baselines. Furthermore, diversity analysis confirms that BERT Mutation preserves structured, meaningful population diversity, avoiding the premature convergence seen in simpler operators.

title: Repopulation Frequency as a Driving Factor in Bias Correction in Asynchronous Parallel Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Asynchronous parallel evolutionary algorithms improve computational efficiency but introduce evaluation-time bias: architectures with shorter evaluation times accumulate disproportionate reproductive opportunity, steering the search toward compact but potentially suboptimal solutions. While correction strategies such as Harada’s frequency-based parent selection and SWEET have been proposed, their behavior in island-based neuroevolution systems with periodic repopulation remains uncharacterized. We present a systematic ablation study comparing these bias correction strategies within EXAMM, a distributed asynchronous neuroevolution framework, across six island repopulation frequencies on three real-world time-series datasets: aviation flight recorder data, coal power plant sensor data and wind turbine sensor data. Each of the 24 experimental conditions is evaluated across 10 independent trials with a fixed budget of 10,000 genome evaluations, with statistical significance assessed via the Mann-Whitney U test against a no-repopulation vanilla baseline. Results show that repopulation frequency provides the strongest effect across the evaluated strategies.

title: Hybrid Multiobjective Evolutionary Search for Realistic Synthetic Face Image Generation
abstract: This article presents a hybrid multiobjective evolutionary algorithm designed to explore the latent space of a Generative Adversarial Network for the production of realistic synthetic human faces. By integrating a Support Vector Machine to identify critical hyperplanes within the latent search space, the method uses problem-dependent knowledge to guide an adaptive Gaussian operator, ensuring demographic diversity and search efficiency. The optimization process simultaneously targets two conflicting objectives: face similarity to a reference identity and specific race attributes. Evaluated against a benchmarking dataset of diverse ages, genders, and races, the proposed approach demonstrated significant improvements over traditional evolutionary baselines, achieving a relative hypervolume increase between 1.4% and 15.4%. The resulting synthetic images successfully deceived state-of-the-art facial recognition systems, highlighting the usefulness of the method in evaluating and enhancing the robustness of biometric security frameworks.

title: Undersampled MRI Reconstruction with Swarm Intelligence
abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) reconstruction from undersampled k-space remains an ill-posed inverse problem, commonly addressed through Fourier-based techniques, regularised optimisation, and data-driven deep learning methods. This study investigates a derivative-free reconstruction approach based on swarm intelligence, focusing on Dispersive Flies Optimisation (DFO) alongside Genetic Algorithms (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO). The proposed framework formulates MRI reconstruction as a frequency-domain optimisation problem, directly minimising masked k-space discrepancy across coils. Experiments are conducted using synthetic multi-coil phantoms under controlled undersampling. Results indicate that, under the tested settings, tuned DFO achieves comparable reconstruction quality to tuned Sensitivity Encoding (SENSE) and Compressed Sensing (CS) baselines in terms of SSIM and PSNR. The findings also highlight a trade-off between reconstruction quality and computational cost, as well as challenges related to multi-coil behaviour and metric alignment. Overall, the study demonstrates the feasibility of swarm-based optimisation for undersampled MRI reconstruction within a controlled setting, and provides a basis for further investigation into statistical robustness, noise sensitivity, and hybrid optimisation strategies.

title: Accelerating Multi-objective Bayesian Optimisation via Predictive-Gradient Catalysts
abstract: This paper presents a general acceleration mechanism for multi-objective Bayesian optimisation (MOBO) that leverages Gaussian process predictive gradients as auxiliary signals. Rather than replacing existing Pareto-compliant acquisition functions, the proposed approach augments them with local stationarity information derived from surrogate-derived gradients, enabling faster convergence toward the global Pareto set under limited evaluation budgets. Two catalyst instantiations are investigated: an adaptive Multiple-Gradient Descent Algorithm-Based Catalyst (MGDA) and a predefined-weight variant that enables focused exploration when budgets are tight. Experiments on the DTLZ benchmark suite (using 2 objectives and 10 decision variables) show that predictive gradient catalysis can deliver significant acceleration compared to other acquisition functions (EHVI, AugTch, tMPoI, SAF) when surrogates are accurate, particularly for stationary problems. (Supplementary material, code, and data are available at Zenodo: 19649281.)

title: Feature and Similarity-Based Explainability of Experimental Materials Data via Black-Box Hyperparameter Optimization
abstract: Building automated pipelines for scientific interpretation of experimental data remains a challenge. We propose a two-stage automated analysis pipeline in which both model-selection steps are formulated as black-box optimization problems over mixed, non-convex hyperparameter spaces and solved with Tree-structured Parzen Estimation (TPE). The first stage explains an automatically tuned Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) regressor with SHAP and permutation feature importance. The second stage extends this parameter-level explainability with cognitively motivated object-level similarity estimation. It extracts stimulus-free similarities from the representations of an automatically tuned classifier trained on functional responses. This extends the approach from the large vision networks domain to small MLPs trained on scarce experimental tabular data. Evaluated on a new solid-foam dataset for pressure-drop and heat-transfer prediction, the pipeline recovers physically meaningful feature attributions and achieves superior or comparable results to a stimulus-based similarity baseline under a physics-informed, overlap-based evaluation.

title: Circuit-Aware Hyperparameter Prediction for MPS Quantum Simulators
abstract: Matrix Product State (MPS) methods are among the most effective approaches for the classical simulation of large-scale quantum circuits, but their practical efficiency depends strongly on hyperparameter settings. These settings can substantially affect both run time and fidelity, and the performance achieved by a given configuration may vary considerably from one circuit to another. Finding suitable settings is itself expensive, since each candidate configuration must be evaluated through circuit simulation. To enable fast circuit-specific MPS hyperparameter selection, we propose a two-stage optimization-plus-learning framework. In the first stage, we perform costly offline single-objective CMA-ES optimization under a fidelity constraint and build a training database. In the second stage, we define circuit features that capture MPS-relevant structural properties and train a circuit-aware hybrid ranking model to rapidly recommend MPS hyperparameter configurations for unseen circuits without additional simulations. We evaluate the approach on multiple scalable circuit families using leave-one-family-out and size-based validation. The results show that offline optimization often improves over default settings, although the magnitude of the gain depends strongly on the backend, circuit family, and circuit scale. The predictor recovers a meaningful fraction of this improvement, performs better under size-based validation than under family-based transfer, and generally remains below the offline optimum.

title: Evolutionary Design of Parameterized Quantum Circuits for Classification and Reinforcement Learning Tasks
abstract: This paper extends Evolutionary eXploration of Augmenting Quantum Circuits (EXAQC), a unified framework for the automated design and optimization of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) to include reinforcement learning tasks. Designing effective quantum circuits is challenging as the performance of a circuit is highly dependent on architecture, including gate composition, qubit interactions, and depth, as well as the target quantum system. Traditional approaches relying on fixed templates or heuristic designs often fail to generalize across tasks. To address this, EXAQC formulates circuit construction as a distributed evolutionary optimization problem, jointly exploring circuit structure and parameters in parallel worker processes using mutation and crossover operators. Experiments on 4 standard classification benchmarks demonstrate that EXAQC achieves competitive or superior accuracy with more efficient circuits. Additionally, evaluations on 4 different reinforcement learning environments show that evolved circuits can learn effective policies and reach near-optimal rewards with relatively low parameter counts. Overall, EXAQC provides a scalable, task-adaptive approach for quantum circuit discovery, highlighting the potential of evolutionary methods in advancing quantum machine learning.

title: Generation of Optimised Quantum Oracles Using Grammar-Based Genetic Programming
abstract: Quantum search algorithms, most notably Grover’s algorithm, offer a significant quadratic speedup over their classical counterparts. The practical realisation of this advantage, however, depends critically on the efficient implementation of a quantum oracle. This oracle functions as a problem-specific “black box”, essential for identifying the desired solutions within the quantum state space. This work tackles the challenge of optimising oracle circuits using grammar-based genetic programming. The objective is to automatically generate circuits that optimise for depth and exhibit greater composability than solutions currently found in the literature. To this end, an abstract grammar was developed to ensure the generation of valid oracles. This grammar is integrated into a genetic programming algorithm that generates circuits. To ensure the validity of each solution, a repair mechanism is applied, and each solution is optimised by a mechanism that removes redundant gates. The evaluation process is based on computing the depth of the generated circuit. The experiments conducted show that the proposed algorithm produces oracles with lower depth than other automatic methods reported in the literature. Oracles were evaluated for conditions such as “less than”, “greater than”, “multiples of”, and “prime numbers”, as well as for complex combinations among them. The results suggest that grammar-based genetic programming is an effective technique for automating the synthesis of valid and efficient quantum oracles.

title: QuantumGS: Quantum Encoding Framework for Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Recent advances in neural rendering, particularly 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), have framed scene reconstruction as a complex iterative optimization problem. However, standard 3DGS relies on classical spherical harmonics, which often struggle to accurately converge on high-frequency, view-dependent effects such as sharp reflections and transparency. While hybrid approaches mitigate this using classical Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), they remain limited by the expressivity of classical networks in low-parameter regimes. In this paper, we bridge the gap between natural computing and rendering by introducing QuantumGS, a novel hybrid framework that integrates Variational Quantum Circuits (VQC), computational models derived from quantum mechanics, into the iterative optimization pipeline of 3DGS. We propose a dedicated unique encoding strategy that maps viewing directions directly onto the Bloch sphere, exploiting the intrinsic geometry of qubit state space to represent three dimensional directional information. Furthermore, we replace classical color modulation networks with quantum circuits instantiated via a hypernetwork or conditioning mechanism. This design increases representational expressivity and improves generalization across the optimization landscape. Source code is available at https://github.com/gwilczynski95/QuantumGS.

title: Tightening the Calculation Gap in Quantum Multi-objective Pseudo-Boolean Optimisation
abstract: Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) is a quantum combinatorial optimiser designed for Single-Objective (SO) problems, and recently extended to Multi-Objective (MO) ones. Its efficiency depends on the parameterisation of its quantum circuit, which requires an iterative interaction between a quantum machine and a classical one. It guarantees solution optimality under extreme-regime configurations, but its quantum-classical interaction overhead is a bottleneck towards practical use even under moderate-efficiency requirements, especially considering today’s costly, noisy, and limited quantum machines. This work attempts to bring the MO-QAOA’s execution to a practical-use scale in low-efficiency regimes, and also quantum advantage in the higher ones. This is done by devising and exploring a Machine Learning (ML)-assisted MO-QAOA that is (I) scalable through parallelisation, (II) extendable to different problems and scalarisations, assisted by (III) generalisable non/neural models, (VI) based on architecture search using an evolutionary linkage-learning algorithm, that (V) considers three feature modelings capturing the problem/circuit properties. (VI) The experiments were conducted on the largest settings in the MO-QAOA literature so far, including problems of 1–5 objectives, 9–156 variables, using 2–11 parallel workers running 9/31-qubit quantum simulators and 4 of the 133/156-qubit largest gate-based quantum machines worldwide. Comparison shows that the ML-assisted MO-QAOA is competitive to the standard MO-QAOA in some cases, and more efficient/faster in others.

title: Developing a Novel Comorbidities Index for Predicting 10-Year Mortality in Prostate Cancer Patients: A Computational Data-Driven Approach
abstract: The Charlson Comorbidities Index (CCI) is a weighted additive index widely used to estimate ten-year mortality risk, but its original weights may not reflect contemporary prognoses. This limitation is critical in Prostate Cancer (PCa), where radical treatment is recommended only for patients with a life expectancy of at least ten years. For candidates eligible for Radical Prostatectomy (RP), accurate estimation of ten-year other-cause mortality is essential to balance oncological benefit against competing risks and avoid overtreatment. We propose a data-driven framework to derive a comorbidity index tailored to PCa patients considered for RP. Using a retrospective single-institution cohort, we apply Population Based Bio-Inspired Algorithm (PBBIAs) to recalibrate comorbidity weights and evolve alternative symbolic formulations optimized for ten-year survival discrimination. We compared six optimization strategies, including symbolic regression approaches based on Genetic Programming (GP), population-based metaheuristics, clinically validated baselines, and survival prediction models. Results show that GA, FST-PSO, and SLIM outperform both the original CCI and the Prostate Cancer specific Comorbidity Index (PCCI), particularly when PCa-specific variables are included, improving the Concordance Index by up to 0.1. GPLearn yields compact and interpretable models with competitive performance. Overall, the proposed approach provides an updated and interpretable tool to improve patient selection for RP.

title: ESTI: Evolutionary Signal and Time-Series Inspection for Auditing ECG Classifiers
abstract: Deep learning has markedly improved automatic electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation, but strong predictive performance does not reveal what evidence a trained classifier treats as sufficient for each diagnosis. We introduce ESTI (Evolutionary Signal and Time-Series Inspection), a model-agnostic framework for globally auditing frozen multi-label ECG classifiers through evolutionary search in a compact, interpretable procedural signal space. Instead of optimizing raw waveforms, ESTI evolves normalized genomes that control meaningful aspects of synthetic 12-lead ECG generation, including beat morphology, rhythm dynamics, lead-dependent structure, and nuisance components. This formulation supports black-box optimization while preserving interpretability at the level of signal-generation factors. Across all abnormalities, the search successfully elicits strong target responses, but these often co-occur with substantial non-target activation, suggesting that the classifier’s decision space is only partially separated. Evolutionary trajectories further show that several class associations arise early and persist throughout optimization, while parameter-drift analyses reveal that some abnormalities depend on focused procedural directions whereas others rely on broader, less isolated regions of the search space. These results position ESTI as a practical method for auditing the internal evidence structure of ECG classifiers, being easily adapted to other signal and time-series classifiers.

title: Evolve While You Train: Online Data Augmentation for Medical Imaging
abstract: Effective deep learning in medical imaging is frequently limited by the lack of large-scale, annotated datasets. While automated data augmentation can improve model generalisation, existing methods often require separate search phases or static policies that are not optimised during training. This paper introduces Data Augmentation Optimiser (DAOP) Online, an evolutionary framework that evolves and optimises data augmentation policies during online model training. By integrating the search process into the training loop, we remove the need for an expensive offline exploration stage. The system employs evolutionary strategies with a snapshot-and-restore mechanism to explore a discrete set of augmentation functions. When combined with continuous probability and magnitude parameters, this creates an effectively infinite search space, all while maintaining the stability of the model weights. The framework was evaluated on the MedMNIST v2 benchmark across various imaging modalities. The results show that DAOP Online consistently identifies modality-specific policies that outperform official baselines and established AutoML methods. We achieved statistically significant improvements in Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) (\(p < 0.05\)), reaching 0.923 for DermaMNIST and 0.956 for PneumoniaMNIST. Furthermore, compared to a projected multi-stage offline evolutionary search, the framework delivers up to a 71% reduction in total GPU-hours. These findings demonstrate that online co-evolution is a practical and efficient solution for automated regularisation in model training.

title: Modularity-Based Linkage Model Assisted Gradient Descent for Neural Network Training
abstract: We present Modularity-based Linkage Model Assisted Gradient Descent (MAGD), which trains feedforward neural networks by alternating short AdamW fine-tunes on a population with a gene-pool optimal-mixing step whose crossover masks are learned online. Each generation aligns a parent and a donor with Git Re-Basin, builds a neuron-level proximity graph from their weight magnitudes, and partitions it with the Leiden community detection algorithm to form a Family of Subsets whose elements serve as crossover masks. AdamW first- and second-moment buffers and a per-individual adaptive learning rate persist across generations, so each network accumulates optimiser context despite recombination. Experiments on the 3-bit MNIST-parity MAGD outperforms an ablation without alignment, a single-model AdamW baseline and a population EA without recombination. A code repository is provided at https://github.com/qyk130/MAGD.

title: Adaptive Protection for Evolutionary Feature Construction in Symbolic Regression with Application to Credit Classification
abstract: Evolutionary feature construction has shown strong promise in symbolic regression by automatically discovering informative transformations of input features that enhance a simple base learner. However, existing approaches often lack explicit mechanisms to preserve important constructed features discovered during evolution, and valuable genetic material can be lost when genetic operators disrupt effective features. This paper introduces an adaptive protection mechanism that leverages feature importance metrics to selectively preserve constructed features during evolution. The mechanism provides stronger protection for more important constructed features while still allowing less important features to be modified and to incorporate useful building blocks from more important features. We evaluate the approach using multiple feature importance calculation methods and demonstrate its robustness across different base learners. Experimental results on 98 regression benchmark datasets show that the proposed mechanism consistently improves solution quality over baseline approaches, and experiments on two credit classification datasets demonstrate that the method also extends effectively to improve search effectiveness beyond symbolic regression.

title: Multi-modal Learning Meets Genetic Programming: Analyzing Alignment in Latent Space Optimization
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) aims to discover mathematical expressions from data, a task traditionally tackled using Genetic Programming (GP) through combinatorial search over symbolic structures. Latent Space Optimization (LSO) methods use neural encoders to map symbolic expressions into continuous spaces, transforming the combinatorial search into continuous optimization. SNIP (Meidani et al., 2024), a contrastive pre-training model inspired by CLIP, advances LSO by introducing a multi-modal approach: aligning symbolic and numeric encoders in a shared latent space to learn the phenotype-genotype mapping, enabling optimization in the numeric space to implicitly guide symbolic search. However, this relies on fine-grained cross-modal alignment, whereas literature on similar models like CLIP reveals that such an alignment is typically coarse-grained. In this paper, we investigate whether SNIP delivers on its promise of effective bi-modal optimization for SR. Our experiments show that: (1) cross-modal alignment does not improve during optimization, even as fitness increases, and (2) the alignment learned by SNIP is too coarse to efficiently conduct principled search in the symbolic space. These findings reveal that while multi-modal LSO holds significant potential for SR, effective alignment-guided optimization remains unrealized in practice, highlighting fine-grained alignment as a critical direction for future work.

title: Prior Coverage and Search Bias in Multiview Symbolic Regression
abstract: Structural prior initialization, which seeds part of the population with templates such as polynomials, trigonometric terms, and rational expressions, dramatically improves symbolic regression (SR), but the dependence on prior quality remains uncharacterized. We study this in multiview SR, which jointly fits several related datasets by decomposing each prediction into a shared core equation and view-specific residuals. We introduce a prior coverage framework characterizing an initialization library along two axes: coverage (the fraction of the target’s structural components the library can represent) and diversity (the breadth of templates beyond target-matching ones). In a factorial study of 3 equation families \(\times \) 7 prior regimes \(\times \) 30 seeds (3,780 runs), we find three behavioral regimes. When the target is reachable (assemblable within the search budget), higher coverage yields lower median loss (Spearman \(\rho = -0.917\), \(p = 0.004\)), and diversity adds further gains at equal coverage (\(p < 0.001\)). When the two trade off, a broad generic library at coverage 0.67 outperforms a narrow matched library at coverage 1.0. On unreachable targets all priors fail and complex templates trap search in local optima. A search-dynamics analysis (450 runs) reveals the mechanisms: seeded-lineage survival does not predict performance, structural diversity collapses by generation 15, and seeded subexpressions (motifs) largely vanish by generation 20: initialization helps by routing search into productive regions, not by preserving seeded structures. Prior effectiveness thus hinges on the interaction of coverage, diversity, and reachability.

title: Strongly-Typed Geometric Syntactic Genetic Programming
abstract: This paper introduces Strongly-Typed Geometric Syntactic Genetic Programming (ST-GSynGP), an extension of Geometric Syntactic Genetic Programming (GSynGP), which is a tree-based Geometric GP variant that leverages geometric crossover in syntactic space to implicitly mitigate bloat and preserve locality. ST-GSynGP improves GSynGP’s applicability for complex problems by accommodating strongly typed and variable-arity functions directly into the geometric crossover mechanism. ST-GSynGP is compared to Strongly-typed Genetic Programming (STGP) across symbolic regression, Boolean logic, classification, and control benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that ST-GSynGP achieves competitive performance while consistently producing more compact and interpretable solutions. These findings demonstrate that combining strong typing with geometric syntactic recombination provides an effective foundation for evolving high-performing and interpretable machine learning models for a wide range of applications.

title: Structure vs. Constants: A Study of Coefficients in Cartesian Genetic Programming
abstract: Cartesian genetic programming (CGP) represents programs as directed acyclic graphs, making it well suited for evolving functional expressions with multiple inputs and outputs. A key yet often overlooked aspect of cartesian genetic programming (CGP) is the role of numerical coefficients, which can significantly influence both the expressiveness and efficiency of evolved solutions. Such coefficients are important not only for improving performance, but also for preventing unnecessary over-complexification of graph structures. In this work, we conduct an extensive study of the role of coefficients in CGP. We investigate multiplicative and additive coefficients applied to nodes or connections and we consider two optimization strategies: Gaussian mutation embedded within the standard CGP mutation process, and gradient-based optimization using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) within a nested optimization loop. To systematically evaluate these design choices, we employ symbolic regression (SR) as a controlled and computationally efficient benchmark. Our results on nine real-world SR datasets show an overall positive impact of coefficients on accuracy, with multiplicative coefficients being more influential than additive ones, and gradient-based optimization consistently outperforming Gaussian mutation. Moreover, we observe that coefficient optimization can often be deferred to a post-processing step with little or no loss in performance.

title: Symbolic Regression for Shared Expressions – Introducing Partial Parameter Sharing
abstract: Symbolic regression aims to find symbolic expressions that describe datasets. Due to its inherent interpretability, Symbolic regression (SR) is a powerful paradigm for scientific discovery. Recent advances have expanded SR to describe related phenomena using a single expression with varying sets of parameters, thereby introducing a single categorical variable. To illustrate, this enables the search for a single expression describing temperature-dependent viscosity across multiple fluids, while simultaneously identifying a distinct set of fluid-specific parameters. We expand upon prior efforts by considering multiple categorical variables and introducing intermediate levels of parameter sharing. Rather than parameters being either entirely universal or entirely unique, some parameters can also be shared across specific categories while remaining distinct for others. This allows for separating universal effects (shared parameters), category-specific trends (partially-shared parameters), and category interactions (non-shared parameters). We test the limits of this setup in terms of reducing data requirements and transfer learning using a synthetic, fitting-only example. Furthermore, we apply the method to an astrophysics dataset also used in a previous single-category study. In comparison, we achieve similar fit quality with significantly fewer parameters while extracting additional information about the problem.

title: Towards ML-Based Position-Aware Mutation Operator in Cartesian Genetic Programming
abstract: Cartesian Genetic Programming (CGP) relies primarily on point mutation, which is uninformed and treats all genes uniformly. Combined with positional bias – nodes near inputs being substantially more likely to be active – most mutations target irrelevant parts of the chromosome. Existing approaches address this by restructuring the genotype; in this paper, the mutation operator itself is made position-aware. The Mean number of Active Output Connections (MAOC), a theoretical metric quantifying positional bias from CGP parameters alone, is derived and validated against an archive of over 11 million mutation records from CGP runs on the PMLB dataset. Three operators of increasing complexity are proposed: probability-based, Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based, and Large Language Model (LLM)-based. Evaluation on 38 symbolic regression tasks shows all three achieve fitness comparable to baseline while accelerating convergence in the early generations of evolutionary search. The probability-based operator reduces runtime by approximately 32 % compared to baseline point mutation, while the GNN-based operator adds runtime overhead of approximately only 21 %.

title: U-Net-Accelerated Quality-Diversity Optimization for Climate-Adaptive Urban Layouts
abstract: Optimizing urban layouts for climate adaptation requires balancing building density with cold-air ventilation. Because physics-based climate simulations are computationally expensive, planners typically evaluate fewer than ten manual designs. Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms offer a way to systematically illuminate the design space, but they require surrogate models to be practical.In this paper, we replace a slow, regulatory physics simulator with a spatial deep-learning surrogate (U-Net) inside an offline MAP-Elites loop. We systematically compare this spatial approach with a traditional Gaussian Process (GP) surrogate across different training-data strategies (quasi-random Sobol sampling vs. active QD bootstrapping). Our results reveal that scalar GP surrogates fail catastrophically when trained on random samples, requiring expensive, actively generated QD archives to generalize. In contrast, the spatial inductive bias of the U-Net allows it to learn the underlying physics mapping robustly (\(R^2 = 0.996\)), completely independent of the training data source. This allows offline QD optimization to achieve highly accurate fitness rankings (\(\rho = 0.994\)) using only a one-time batch of random training samples. The resulting pipeline, deployed in the open-source OpenSKIZZE tool, generates thousands of diverse, climate-evaluated building layouts in under ten minutes.

title: GP-GOMEA with GPU-Based Fitness Evaluations: Design and Performance Analysis
abstract: GP-GOMEA is a state-of-the-art evolutionary algorithm for symbolic regression, known for discovering small and interpretable models. However, its computational cost remains substantial, limiting its applicability to larger datasets and more complex target expressions. In contrast, the rise of modern subsymbolic approaches, particularly deep learning, has been driven largely by the massive parallelism offered by GPUs. In this work, we take the first major step toward a fully GPU-accelerated GP-GOMEA by introducing a GPU-based fitness evaluation scheme. We design a GPU-friendly representation of GP-GOMEA’s template-based individuals and a corresponding evaluation strategy that exploits the inherent parallelism of population-based search. This substantially increases evaluation throughput, enabling orders of magnitude more evaluations within the same time budget. Across four standard symbolic regression benchmarks, this increased evaluation capacity yields performance improvements, particularly for larger datasets and larger population sizes. Moreover, the ability to efficiently evaluate much larger datasets and more complex templates enables analyses that were previously infeasible, allowing us to systematically analyze what makes expressions increasingly difficult for GP-GOMEA, providing new insights into how expression structure affects search difficulty. Finally, for the first time, this expanded capability allows a problem-agnostic evolutionary algorithm to reliably regress one of the largest Feynman equations within four hours.

title: Reshaping the Fitness Landscape of Classification Rule Mining for Clinical Natural Language Processing
abstract: Clinical texts are valuable sources of patient information, but they are hard to process automatically due to synonyms, abbreviations, and terminological variability. Classification rule mining can extract readable “IF-THEN” rules that clinicians can understand and verify. Standard evolutionary rule miners rely on exact word matching, which fails when the same concept is expressed with different words (e.g., “renal failure” vs. “kidney failure”). This fragments the fitness landscape into vast neutral plateaus where standard operators cannot progress.We propose a multi-objective evolutionary framework that integrates word embeddings into binary classification rule mining at two levels: soft matching, which allows semantically similar terms to contribute to rule coverage during fitness evaluation, and a semantic mutation operator, which replaces terms with embedding-space neighbors during search. Together, these components restore a continuous optimization gradient in place of the flat landscape caused by terminological variability.Experiments on MIMIC-IV-Note across five diagnostic targets show that our framework more than doubles the mean hypervolume (+116%) and substantially improves the F1-score (+80%) compared to exact-matching baseline NSGA-II and bitflip mutation, while maintaining fully interpretable rule structures. Fitness landscape analysis confirms that the combined approach reduces neutrality and increases information content, explaining its superior search dynamics.

title: Multi-objective Coevolution of Prompts and Templates for Circuit Approximation
abstract: Approximate multipliers deliberately relax computational accuracy to achieve gains in power efficiency, latency, and silicon area, which makes them well-suited for error-resilient applications such as neural networks. In this work, we introduce a co-evolutionary algorithm that leverages an off-the-shelf large language model (LLM) without requiring domain-specific training to automate the design of optimized 8-bit approximate multipliers. The approach simultaneously evolves a population of candidate circuits and a population of prompt templates that steer LLM-driven modifications. Experimental results for several target design objectives demonstrate that the proposed method discovers approximate multipliers with improved error–area trade-offs compared to highly optimized circuits from the EvoApproxLib library.

title: Data Centric AutoML Embedding Optimisation for Mode of Delivery Prediction
abstract: Multimodal learning pipelines increasingly rely on high-dimensional embedding representations extracted from pre-trained models. However, these embedding spaces often contain redundancy and noise, which can hinder the learning process. In this work, we reformulate multimodal learning as a data-centric optimisation problem, where the goal is to jointly optimise feature selection, instance selection and model choice in embedding space. To this end, we adopt the Evolutionary Data-Centric AutoML (EDCA) framework to operate directly over multimodal embeddings, treated as structured data, enabling the automatic search for efficient predictive pipelines. The proposed approach is evaluated on a real-world clinical application for predicting mode of delivery following Induction of Labour (IOL). The multimodal data combines maternal-fetal tabular clinical data and third-trimester ultrasound images. Their embeddings are extracted from a pre-trained multimodal model and organised into multiple configurations, which are then optimised using EDCA. Results show that this approach can achieve comparable average performance to multimodal architectures and occasionally identify better configurations, relying on selected subsets of samples and features, which shows that performance improvements can be driven by data quality rather than model complexity. These findings highlight the effectiveness of EDCA for optimising representations and support its suitability for complex multimodal problems in real-world applications.

title: NEATWork: A Spatial Network Optimizer
abstract: NASA’s planned sustained presence of humans on the Moon will require significant volumes of icy regolith transport across the lunar surface. Algorithmic planning of efficient spatial transport networks connecting multiple terminals and optimizing across a range of objectives remains an open challenge. To address this problem, we developed NEATWork, a spatial network planner. By modifying the well-known NEAT genetic algorithm—traditionally used for the development of neural networks—we present a graph optimization approach that can take into account various spatial and topological objectives. We illustrate our solution using the case of lunar transport network planning, though it can be easily deployed in other network planning scenarios where spatial cost maps can be made and the flexibility for a black box cost function optimization is of interest. We provide two open-source implementations.

title: Evolutionary Bi-objective Optimization for Safer Student Cycling Routes: Algorithmic Design and Real-World Validation
abstract: Urban route planning for student cyclists involves balancing safety and environmental exposure in complex metropolitan areas. In cities like Mexico City, cyclists face both high levels of air pollution and elevated crime risks as they navigate dense urban environments. This study formulates a bi-objective routing problem designed to minimize crime risk and air pollution exposure using real-world data sources. A large-scale bicycle network has been constructed around a university-centered area, incorporating multiple destinations relevant to student mobility. The proposed framework is evaluated across 30 origin-destination instances, systematically grouped by distance from the starting point, to analyze performance at various spatial scales. As a deterministic baseline, a Multiobjective Dijkstra Algorithm is employed to compute the exact Pareto fronts. To enhance computational scalability, two evolutionary multiobjective approaches based on NSGA-II are introduced. These methods include a novel path-preserving mutation operator that maintains route feasibility while improving exploration of the search space. Experimental results show that the proposed evolutionary approaches provide high-quality approximations of the exact Pareto fronts with significantly lower computational costs, emphasizing their suitability for large-scale, real-world routing applications.

title: DASOF-HSI: Dual-Stage Adaptive Subset Optimization Framework via Improved Harmony Search for Multimodal Mild Cognitive Impairment Detection
abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) can benefit from multimodal digital assessment, but the resulting feature space and ensemble construction process often contain substantial redundancy. To address this issue, we organize model construction for multimodal MCI detection into two coordinated binary subset optimization stages, one for multimodal feature selection and the other for base-learner selection in stacking. Based on this design, we propose DASOF-HSI, a dual-stage adaptive subset optimization framework built on an improved Harmony Search strategy. In the first stage, a compact subset is selected from electrodermal activity, inter-beat interval signals, and digital cognitive-task features, with the search adaptively regulated by harmony-memory diversity. In the second stage, the optimized feature space is fixed and a compact subset of base learners is selected for stacking, where adaptation is guided by learner quality together with memory diversity. Experiments on a dataset of 1,069 older adults show that DASOF-HSI achieves an accuracy of 0.885, a precision of 0.891, a recall of 0.887, and an F1-score of 0.889, outperforming all compared baselines. Comparisons with alternative subset optimization strategies and ablation analyses further show that the proposed framework improves predictive performance under a controlled evaluation protocol while retaining compact feature and learner subsets.

title: Surrogate Prediction of Evolutionary Algorithm Tournaments for Traffic Model Calibration
abstract: Surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithms (SAEAs) are commonly used to reduce the cost of optimisation when objective function evaluations are expensive, such as in traffic model calibration. Traditional approaches approximate the objective function using regression models or rank the full population. However, many evolutionary algorithms rely on tournament selection, which only requires relative comparisons between a few candidate solutions rather than accurate fitness estimates or full population ranking. This observation motivates an alternative surrogate approach based on pairwise ranking. Tournament selection can be decomposed into binary comparisons of the form: is one solution fitter than another? This enables the use of surrogate models that directly predict tournament outcomes. In this work, we propose tournament prediction surrogates, both classification and regression forms, and compare with standard fitness approximation surrogates. Experiments on three continuous benchmark problems and a real-world traffic calibration problem with 1,574 parameters demonstrate tournament-based surrogates offer advantages in high-dimensional settings.

title: Generation of Diverse and Functional Robot Designs Using Superquadrics Parametrisation and Quality-Diversity
abstract: Generative design of robots requires navigating a vast search-space, encompassing physical configurations and behavioural parameters. Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) have shown promising results, but often converge prematurely to a small set of sub-optimal designs. To counter premature convergence, we introduce a superquadrics-based representation (SQs) for robot bodies. SQs are interpretable, compact and computationally efficient mathematical representations of 3D geometrical shapes that can be tuned to specific design-spaces. To encourage morphological diversity, we combine this representation with a quality-diversity (QD) algorithm (MAP-Elites). We compare SQs and Compositional Pattern Producing Networks representations as generators of morphologies, combining them with standard EAs and MAP-Elites. In two test environments, we find that using SQs to generate morphology in conjunction with the MAP-Elites algorithm reaches the highest QD-score across both environments, maximising diversity of design and functionality of generated robots. The findings highlight the benefits of using a compact and interpretable geometric representation for exploring a complex design-space and suggest that combining SQs with an explicit diversity mechanism increases the quality and number of designs generated.

title: Quality Diversity for Reliable Data Driven Time-Use Optimization
abstract: The daily allocation of the finite 24-h time budget is strongly associated with physical, mental, and cognitive health. While predictive models can estimate the relationship between time-use compositions and health outcomes such as body mass index, life satisfaction, and cognition, most optimization approaches focus only on maximizing expected benefit and do not consider the uncertainty inherent in data-driven prediction. Ignoring uncertainty in health-related decisions can lead to unrealistic time-use recommendations. To address this gap, we introduce an uncertainty quantification Quality Diversity (QD) framework for a more reliable time-use recommendation. Objective functions are derived using compositional data analysis using a large child cohort dataset \(n > 1000\), to capture the relationship between daily activity compositions and multiple health indicators. We develop a new approach that incorporates predictive uncertainty into QD processes and produces more reliable recommendations that balance the expected health benefits with the confidence of the model. We explore the solution space through variable-based and objective-based behavioral representations, revealing diverse high-quality time-use composition and explicit relationships between health outcomes under uncertainty. By embedding uncertainty directly into optimization, our framework shifts the time-use recommendations toward regions of lower uncertainty while preserving high-quality structures for more reliable decision-making in behavioral health.

title: A New Encoding to Mitigate Representation Biases in Morphological Robot Evolution
abstract: Modular robot morphologies in evolutionary robotics are frequently represented using Compositional Pattern Producing Networks (CPPNs) decoded via breadth-first search (BFS). We identify and analyse a previously overlooked representational bias of this approach causing evolved populations converge to hinge-dominated body plans. We also show that CPPN-based encodings exhibit rotation non-invariance, substantial memory overhead, and genotypes that are resistant to compression. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel representation, Neural Developmental Encoding (NDE) with highest-probability decoding (HPD), where morphologies are derived from connection probability matrices produced by a fixed decoder network operating on compact embedding vectors. Our experiments reveal that NDE+HPD significantly outperforms CPPN+BFS, achieving a 40% increase in fitness and a 32% boost in population diversity, while reducing the average hinge-to-module ratio from 0.99 to 0.68. Thus, this study resolves a previously unnoticed bias in CPPNs and provides quantitative evidence that the choice of genetic encoding is a crucial design decision, as it profoundly shapes the set of morphologies that evolution can search and discover.

title: GSAM: A Generalizable and Safe Robotic Framework for Articulated Object Manipulation
abstract: Articulated object manipulation is a unique challenge for service robots. Existing methods employ end-to-end policy learning, vision-motion planning, and large-language/visual-language model (LLM/VLM), but often overlook the diversity of articulated objects and the complexity of interactions between end-effector and handle, leading to limited generalization and destructive collisions. To address this, we propose GSAM, a generalizable and safe robotic framework for articulated object manipulation. Specifically, a vision-based perceiver generates the kinematic parameters. Considering that pre-trained markers in perceiver yield raw estimations that may deviate from commonsense, we present a fine-tuned VLM-based refiner, using chain-of-thought (COT) commonsense reasoning to refine perception. To prevent destructive collisions, we design an interaction constraint function generator, integrating articulated object, interaction pose, and obstacle avoidance knowledge into a base. LLM then functionalize these constraints and apply them to trajectory and posture planning. A kinematic-aware manipulation planner verifies reachability for trajectory and posture. Experiments on 50 hinge tasks across 5 object categories and 50 randomly initialized end-effector-handle configurations show that GSAM reduces standard deviation by 3.1% and improves manipulation success rate by 36.0% compared to the best baseline, respectively demonstrating the superior object generalization and interaction safety of GSAM in practical scenarios.

title: Lens-Descriptor Guided Evolutionary Algorithm for Optimization of Complex Optical Systems with Glass Choice
abstract: Fixed-structure lens design is a high-dimensional mixed integer problem with many local minima: radii and distances are continuous, glass choices are discrete, and in practice, designers need a portfolio of strong alternatives rather than a single optimum. We address this challenge with the novel Lens-Descriptor Guided Evolutionary Algorithm (LDG-EA), a parallel multimodal optimization method for fixed-structure optical design with explicit glass choice. LDG-EA turns an optics notion of structural similarity into a search primitive: it partitions the design space into interpretable descriptor classes defined by radius-sign patterns and glass identities, learns which classes are promising, and runs descriptor-constrained searches in parallel. This makes diversity explicit, allocation of computational resources efficient, and the search naturally scalable on modern parallel hardware. On the six-element Double-Gauss benchmark, LDG-EA outperforms the considered quality-diversity, multimodal, and lens-specific baselines in runtime, diversity, and solution quality under the same computational budget . Across five runs, it identifies more than 400 high-quality local-minimum candidates on average and, in total over five runs, finds 403 designs that outperform the locally optimized Double-Gauss reference lens. These results position LDG-EA as a practical route to time-to-portfolio optimization in optics for the Double-Gauss structure and as a promising template for search in other structured engineering design problems.

title: Morphological Evolution of Aerial Robots: Comparing Genetic Encodings
abstract: Evolutionary robotics has long debated direct versus generative encodings, but most evidence comes from terrestrial and aquatic robots, where imperfect morphologies still yield functional (albeit poor) behaviour and thus useful fitness signal. Aerial robots differ in that the boundary between functional and nonfunctional designs is sharp, and small morphological changes can produce configurations incapable of hovering. This motivates our study on encodings in a domain where the border between viable and non-viable designs is sharp. We evolve hexacopter morphologies using direct, indirect, and hybrid encodings, combined with a geometric controller individually tuned to each morphology, and compare them under standard and speciation-based evolution. Without speciation, CPPN-based methods outperform direct encoding. With speciation, this trend reverses. We attribute the CPPN drop to low-locality mutations producing scattered offspring that speciation fails to refine. Overall, the hybrid encoding is the most robust across settings.

title: Pattern Layout Optimization for Seam-Aware Texture Alignment
abstract: When assembling a garment from patterned fabric, periodic motifs such as stripes or checks should continue seamlessly across seam lines, yet the two subproblems involved, nesting (minimising fabric waste) and texture alignment (matching pattern phase at seams), are mostly studied in isolation. Prior texture-alignment work assumes an unbounded fabric supply and deforms 2D patch shapes directly, leaving garment fit changes implicit and unmeasured. We propose the first joint optimisation of fabric efficiency, seam-wise texture alignment, and fit preservation. Our key idea is to optimise seam positions on the 3D body mesh rather than deforming flat patterns: this grounds every modification in body geometry, making fit deviation an explicit, measurable objective. Texture periodicity is modelled via wallpaper symmetry groups, covering eight pattern families including herringbone, chevron, and brick bond. We solve the resulting mixed search space (continuous seam parameters, discrete phase offsets, grain orientations) with a mixed-integer evolution strategy using variable-specific operators. Experiments on three garment types with up to 2,200 pattern pieces show consistent improvement in texture alignment over all baselines including random search at matched evaluation budget.

title: Efficient Imitation-Based Rule Learning for Online Yard Crane Scheduling via Order-Aware Geometric Semantic Genetic Programming
abstract: Genetic Programming (GP) for evolving scheduling rules often relies on expensive simulation-based evaluations, which provide limited guidance and may lead to slow convergence. Existing research mitigates expensive simulation through instance subsampling or surrogate evaluation, but subsampling often yields noisy and unstable fitness signals, whereas surrogate models heavily rely on previously seen samples for accurate prediction. In this work, imitating near-optimal decision-point-wise behaviour to explicitly guide scheduling rule learning to speed up convergence is explored. Since such target behaviour is not readily available, a method is proposed to derive near-optimal target behaviour on representative decision points. As scheduling rules select actions by comparing rule-generated scores, making relative orderings more important than absolute output values, the derived target behaviour is naturally expressed via action orderings. This makes Order-aware Geometric Semantic GP (O-GSGP) a natural fit for searching effectively in this ordering-behaviour semantic space. In addition, since interpretability is important in scheduling rule learning, an ordering-behaviour-preserving pruning mechanism is introduced to control rule growth induced by geometric semantic operators. Experiments on the online Yard Crane scheduling problem show that the resulting scheduling-adapted O-GSGP achieves better average performance than standard GP and several advanced acceleration methods when the guiding target semantics are computationally cheap, behaviourally general, and strong.

title: Informative Decision Situation Selection for Phenotypic Characterization-Based Surrogate-Assisted Genetic Programming in Dynamic Container Terminal Truck Scheduling
abstract: Surrogate-assisted genetic programming (SAGP) addresses the computational challenge of evolving heuristics for dynamic scheduling by replacing expensive fitness evaluations with learned approximations. However, standard surrogate models require fixed-size inputs, whereas GP individuals are variable-sized symbolic programs, making characterization a core challenge. Phenotypic characterization (PC) observes each individual’s behavior over a selected set of decision situations (DSs), where each DS captures a scheduling decision moment and its candidate actions. The selected DSs therefore determine what behavioral evidence is available to the surrogate model. Existing studies typically use fixed DS sets that are randomly sampled or left unspecified, leaving the construction of informative DS sets under a fixed observation budget as an open question. In this paper, we study informative DS selection for PC-based SAGP in dynamic container terminal truck scheduling (DCTTS). We develop a multi-stage framework that first collects a broad raw DS pool using committee policies and constructs a representative candidate pool, then applies Alignment-Guided Quality-Coverage Greedy (AQCG) to select complementary DSs within this observation budget. AQCG measures DS informativeness by quantifying how well each DS’s induced behavioral distinctions align with true performance differences, then greedily maximizes set-level coverage of this alignment information. Experimental results on DCTTS show that AQCG achieves the best overall scheduling performance among the compared methods and improves surrogate guidance over random sampling and quality-only selection.
